guard_patterns.handling: Require an official public source surface.
Keep meter, measured, calculated and estimated data distinct.
Keep national, local-authority, site and parcel geographies distinct.
Retain calendar period, meter period, publication edition and revision notices.
Do not treat energy or traffic activity as emissions without an explicit conversion method.
Keep permitted activity and site reporting scope explicit.
Keep UK ETS free allocation, verified emissions and surrendered allowances distinct.
Keep CO2, CH4, N2O and CO2e semantics explicit.
Carry official correction and revision notices downstream.
No parcel value without geometry, identity and activity binding.

packages.title: DESNZ subnational electricity meter and sector coverage QA
facts: DESNZ publishes electricity-consumption estimates at region and local-authority level in Great Britain.
The 2005 to 2024 series is National Statistics.
The statistics separate domestic and non-domestic consumption.
The statistics also provide total consumption.
They report the number of electricity meters.
They report mean consumption per meter.
They report median consumption per meter.
The 2024 tables were published in the December 2025 update.
These are consumption statistics rather than direct greenhouse-gas measurements.
Local-authority electricity statistics are not parcel-level measurements.

packages.title: DESNZ onsite-generation coverage gap QA
facts: The 2024 subnational electricity report is based on meter-level consumption data.
Electricity data aggregators compile meter data on behalf of suppliers.
Domestic properties can have onsite electricity generation.
Non-domestic properties can also have onsite electricity generation.
Solar panels are an example of onsite generation identified by DESNZ.
Wind turbines are another example identified by DESNZ.
Some onsite generation is exported to the grid.
Some onsite generation is consumed directly onsite.
Electricity consumed directly from onsite generation is not captured by the meter-based collection described by DESNZ.
Metered local electricity consumption must not be treated as complete parcel energy use where onsite generation is unknown.

packages.title: DESNZ electricity meter-period time-base QA
facts: DESNZ gives a specific time basis for 2024 non-half-hourly meter estimates.
Non-half-hourly estimates cover February 2024 to January 2025.
DESNZ gives a different time basis for half-hourly meter estimates.
Half-hourly estimates cover January to December 2024.
The publication combines these meter classes in subnational reporting.
The statistics are presented by consuming sector.
The statistics are presented by geographic area.
Calendar labels therefore do not imply an identical raw-meter interval for every meter class.
Time-base differences should be retained in downstream provenance.
The time-base distinction does not create a parcel greenhouse-gas measurement.

packages.title: DESNZ subnational gas domestic/non-domestic coverage QA
facts: DESNZ publishes gas-consumption statistics for regions and local authorities in Great Britain.
The statistics include domestic gas consumption.
The statistics include non-domestic gas consumption.
They also include total gas consumption.
The current data family includes 2024 consumption tables.
DESNZ provides non-weather-corrected subnational gas statistics.
The subnational summary provides local-authority gas tables.
The summary also provides smaller-area gas tables for domestic consumption.
Gas consumption is activity data and is not itself CO2e.
Local-authority gas consumption must not be represented as a parcel emission without parcel activity binding.

packages.title: DESNZ gas-statistics revision provenance QA
facts: DESNZ revised historical gas tables on 5 May 2026.
That revision addressed a processing error affecting some Welsh local authorities.
The affected historical period was 2005 to 2013.
The error assigned data against incorrect local authorities.
Total figures for Wales were not affected by that allocation error.
DESNZ also revised the tables on 19 December 2025.
The December 2025 correction concerned non-domestic gas consumption for one North East area.
That correction affected 2023 data.
Official revision notices must be carried into downstream evidence.
Older local-authority values should not silently replace the corrected edition.

packages.title: Environment Agency Pollution Inventory site and permit boundary QA
facts: The Pollution Inventory covers releases and transfers from regulated industrial activities in England.
Reporting is annual for the previous calendar year.
Operators of multiple sites need a separate return for each site.
A site with several permits can require separate reporting for permitted activities.
The Environment Agency instructs operators to report emissions from the permit being reported.
Operators should not add unrelated permitted activities into a return.
The reporting process identifies relevant pollutants and emission sources.
It includes direct and fugitive emissions where applicable.
A Pollution Inventory site record is regulatory-site evidence, not proof of parcel ownership.
Parcel attribution requires a separate geometry and identity match.

packages.title: Environment Agency Pollution Inventory threshold and BRT QA
facts: Pollution Inventory returns cover applicable pollutants from regulated activities.
The return can contain an actual release value.
Where applicable it can contain 'brt' for below relevant threshold.
Above a reporting threshold the total annual mass released or transferred is reported.
Below-threshold emissions may be recorded as 'brt' instead of a numeric value.
The Environment Agency encourages actual values when they are available.
The reporting table distinguishes substances and environmental media.
Threshold reporting does not mean a below-threshold emission is zero.
A 'brt' code must not be converted into a fabricated numeric emission.
Threshold semantics must be preserved before any candidate scoring.

packages.title: Environment Agency release-estimation technique QA
facts: The Environment Agency prefers site-specific data where mandatory methodologies are unavailable.
Monitored emission concentrations can support site-specific quantification.
Mass-balance techniques can also support quantification where appropriate.
Certified equipment or accredited services are preferred for measured concentrations.
Continuous monitoring is normally preferred over periodic sampling.
Site-specific emission factors are preferred over generic representative-plant factors.
Emission factors relate emissions to an activity within the process.
Significant abnormal operating events can require separate estimation.
Different release-estimation techniques have different evidence strength.
An estimated regulated-site release must not be labelled as a direct parcel measurement.

packages.title: UK ETS registry allocation versus emissions QA
facts: The UK ETS Registry publishes public reports.
It publishes installation-operator account-holder and allocation information.
The 2026 registry report was published on 5 July 2026.
The public allocation reports include free UK allowance allocations.
The DESNZ allocation table covers the 2021 to 2026 allocation period.
Free allocation is intended to reduce carbon-leakage risk for eligible operators.
Activity-level changes can amend free allocations.
A free allocation is an allowance quantity, not the installation's measured greenhouse-gas emission.
Installation identity can support a point-source candidate.
Registry allocation data must remain distinct from parcel emission values.

packages.title: UK ETS compliance emissions and surrender QA
facts: The UK ETS Registry publishes a compliance report covering emissions and surrendered allowances.
The current public compliance report covers scheme years 2021 to 2025.
That report was published on 22 June 2026.
UK ETS annual emissions reports are independently verified for covered operators.
Covered operators surrender allowances against reportable emissions under scheme rules.
Emissions and surrendered allowances are separate report fields and concepts.
A compliance account can identify a regulated installation or operator.
Verified scheme emissions are stronger evidence than an allowance allocation for reported emissions.
Scheme emissions still follow the regulated installation boundary.
They cannot be assigned to a land parcel without site-to-parcel binding.

packages.title: UK ETS verifier and installation-scope QA
facts: UK ETS accredited verifiers verify annual emissions reports.
Verification applies to covered installations.
Verification also applies to covered aircraft operators.
Verification now also applies to maritime operators under the scheme rules.
UKAS accredits UK ETS verifiers for specific scopes.
Installation coverage includes specified regulated greenhouse-gas activities.
Combustion installations can enter scope where total rated thermal input exceeds 20 MW, subject to scheme exclusions.
Northern Ireland electricity generators remain in the EU ETS under the relevant arrangements.
Verifier accreditation strengthens report assurance but does not change the installation boundary.
A verified installation report is not automatically a parcel-level measurement.

packages.title: Defra agricultural nitrous-oxide source QA
facts: Agriculture accounted for 59% of UK nitrous-oxide emissions in 2024 in Defra's 2025 agri-environment release.
Agricultural nitrous oxide was about 12 MtCO2e in 2024 in that release.
The comparable 1990 agricultural nitrous-oxide estimate was about 16 MtCO2e.
Defra describes agricultural nitrous-oxide emissions as having fallen by about 26% since 1990.
Soils are the majority source of agricultural nitrous oxide.
Nitrogen fertiliser application is an important source process.
Applied manure is an important source process.
Manure excreted on pasture is also identified.
Leaching and run-off contribute to agricultural nitrous-oxide emissions.
National agricultural source shares are not field- or parcel-level measurements.

packages.title: Defra agricultural methane source QA
facts: Agriculture accounted for 49% of UK methane emissions in 2024 in Defra's 2025 agri-environment release.
Agricultural methane was about 27 MtCO2e in 2024.
The comparable 1990 agricultural methane estimate was about 33 MtCO2e.
Defra describes agricultural methane as having fallen by about 18% since 1990.
Enteric fermentation is the majority agricultural methane source.
Ruminating animals are central to enteric-fermentation emissions.
Manure-management practices account for the remainder described by Defra.
Lower livestock numbers are identified as the main driver of the long-term methane reduction.
Methane must remain distinct from nitrous oxide and carbon dioxide in source evidence.
National livestock-source evidence does not identify emissions from an individual parcel.

packages.title: Defra agriculture inventory-revision guard QA
facts: Defra's 2025 agriculture release states that agriculture is around 13% of UK greenhouse-gas emissions.
The release reports methane, nitrous oxide and carbon dioxide separately.
Agriculture's carbon-dioxide share is much smaller than its methane and nitrous-oxide shares.
The release states that greenhouse-gas inventory data are revised each year.
Methodological improvements can change historical inventory values.
The 2025 release therefore supersedes older agriculture headline shares for equivalent comparisons.
Sector shares can change because agricultural emissions change.
Sector shares can also change because non-agricultural emissions change.
Year and inventory edition must be preserved with agriculture evidence.
Revision-aware national evidence still does not supply parcel emissions.

packages.title: DfT 2025 road-type traffic QA
facts: DfT reports Great Britain road traffic by road type.
A-road traffic was 151.6 billion vehicle miles in 2025.
A-road traffic increased 1.9% from 2024.
Minor-road traffic was 119.0 billion vehicle miles in 2025.
Minor-road traffic increased 1.5% from 2024.
Motorway traffic was 71.9 billion vehicle miles in 2025.
Motorway traffic increased 2.4% from 2024.
The corresponding 2024 road-type values are published in the same series.
Road-type activity can improve transport-model context.
National road traffic totals are not parcel emissions.

packages.title: DfT traffic-activity versus emissions QA
facts: The DfT road-traffic surface reports vehicle miles travelled.
Vehicle miles are transport activity rather than greenhouse-gas mass.
The source separates A-roads, minor roads and motorways.
Road-type activity changes can affect modeled transport emissions.
Converting traffic activity to emissions requires additional emission-factor and fleet information.
The traffic series alone does not identify fuel consumed on a specific parcel.
The traffic series alone does not measure tailpipe emissions at a parcel.
Traffic activity and DESNZ local-road emissions therefore have different semantics.
Activity evidence can be used as a cross-check without replacing emissions evidence.
Parcel transport emissions remain null without a defensible spatial and methodological binding.

packages.title: ONS territorial, residence and footprint basis QA
facts: ONS describes three main UK greenhouse-gas measurement bases.
The three bases are territorial, residence and footprint.
Territorial emissions cover emissions occurring within UK borders.
Residence emissions align with the UK National Accounts.
Footprint emissions are a consumption-based measure.
ONS reports estimated 2025 UK territorial emissions of 367 MtCO2e in its July 2026 methodology summary.
That territorial headline is described as 54% lower than 1990.
ONS reports provisional 2024 production/residence emissions of 478 MtCO2e.
That residence headline is described as 42% lower than 1990.
The three bases are valid for different purposes and must not be silently substituted for one another or for parcel measurements.

packages.title: DESNZ LULUCF gas-separation and land-process QA
facts: DESNZ reports separate 2024 LULUCF estimates for carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide.
The 2024 UK LULUCF carbon-dioxide estimate is a net removal in the cited methodology.
The cited 2024 carbon-dioxide figure is about -6,761.78 Gg CO2.
The cited 2024 methane figure is about 5,745.64 Gg CO2e.
The cited 2024 nitrous-oxide figure is about 1,300.99 Gg CO2e.
DESNZ identifies methane from drained and rewetted organic soils among LULUCF processes.
Nitrous oxide can arise from nitrogen fertilisation of new forests and soil mineralisation following land-use change.
Non-CO2 emissions from agricultural land due to agricultural activities such as fertilisation are reported in the Agriculture sector rather than duplicated in LULUCF.
Gas identity and sector assignment therefore matter in land-use evidence.
National or local LULUCF methodology outputs do not by themselves create a measured parcel emission.
